newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS-Dyno profits jump 40 percent in H1.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dyno profits jump 40 percent in H1.

text.p: Norwegian explosives and chemicals producer Dyno Industrier ASA said on Monday improved market conditions and the effects of a restructuring programme had led to a 40 percent rise in first half pre-tax profits.
The Oslo-based group beat market expectations to book profits before tax of 262 million crowns ($35.5 million) in the first half compared with 187 million crowns in the same year-ago period.
Operating profits rose 23 percent to 300 million crowns versus 244 million crowns.

"I am very pleased with the result so far this year," Dag Mejdell, Dyno's cheif executive officer, said in a statement. "A number of improvement measures which are planned under the Dyno 2000 profitability programme are currently being implemented, and I view the corporation's future prospects with optimism."
Dyno said, however, that the second quarter was seasonally the best quarter of the year and it saw no significant changes in the group's business conditions in the remainder of 1997.
"Accordingly, quarterly profits in the second half of the year are not expected to be of the same order as those reported in the second quarter," the company said.

Dyno Nobel, the explosives division, was expected to report favourable figures as a result of continuing good markets. Second-quarter operating profits for explosives rose 57 percent to 121 million crowns from 77 million crowns a year ago.
Dyno said the increase was largely due to the Dyno 2000 programme and higher demand for its products. Margins also were lifted by a fall in feedstock ammonia prices, it said.
Second-quarter operating profit for chemicals improved to 94 million crowns against 55 million crowns, largely as a result of higher volumes and an increase in the contract price for methanol.
The contract price for methanol was 344 marks per tonne in the second quarter versus 225 marks per tonne in the same 1996 period. The third-quarter price has been set at 330 marks per tonne.
Dyno attributed a three percent decline in operating revenues in its plastics division in the first six months to reduced demand for industrial packaging and fewer deliveries of transport systems.
Operating profits for plastics fell to 29 million crowns compared with 51 million in the first half 1996.

"The prices of key plastic raw materials continued to rise throughout the second quarter, exerting pressure on margins," Dyno said. "No significant increase in the price of plastic raw materials is expected in the coming period."
